question: Can abrupt behavioral changes in language models be detected automatically from their output distributions without hand-designing a task-specific order parameter?

key_findings.claim: The method treats a phase transition as a local maximum in an f-divergence between output distributions on the two sides of a control parameter.
key_findings.evidence: It derives total-variation, Jensen-Shannon and a low-variance linear dissimilarity estimator using sampled text and tractable autoregressive probabilities. In the local small-step limit, smooth g-dissimilarities reduce to Fisher information.

key_findings.claim: Prompt scans reveal both semantic and tokenizer-induced transitions.
key_findings.evidence: Instruction-tuned Mistral/Llama models show a peak at the threshold in an integer comparison prompt while tested base models do not. Pythia instead shows a sharp output change around 2020/2021 that coincides with its number-tokenization boundary, demonstrating that peaks need not correspond to a learned capability.

key_findings.claim: Temperature sweeps exhibit frozen, coherent and disordered regimes, but the high-temperature feature may be a finite-system crossover.
key_findings.evidence: For Pythia-70M and one OpenWebText prompt, peaks occur near 0.02 and 0.5 using 20,480 ten-token generations per temperature. The second transition also appears in a unigram model, and autoregressive greedy conditioning yields a negative heat-capacity analogue.

key_findings.claim: Checkpoint analysis finds prompt-dependent output changes, but several sharp peaks are isolated outliers rather than persistent macroscopic phases.
key_findings.evidence: Across Pythia checkpoints, output dissimilarities overlap some weight-distribution changes around 80K steps. Short prompts also peak around 20K and 40K, yet adjacent points return to prior behavior; larger comparison windows suppress these outliers.

method.core_idea: Detect behavioral change points by estimating generic statistical distances between full generated-text distributions across neighboring regions of a tunable parameter.
method.mechanism: Choose a control parameter and window length, sample autoregressive outputs at grid points, score each output under left/right mixture distributions, estimate linear/TV/JS dissimilarity, and flag local maxima for semantic follow-up.
assumptions: The selected prompts and output length expose behavior of interest.
The autoregressive model provides calibrated enough sequence probabilities for distance estimation.
Abrupt distributional change is a useful operational definition of transition.
Sampling and grid resolution are sufficient to separate persistent changes from noise or isolated checkpoints.

techniques.role: Measures distributional change without task-specific correctness labels.
Controls the scale at which a change counts as persistent.
Cross-checks temperature peaks using an energy derivative.

evaluations.setting: Integer prompts across Pythia, Mistral and Llama-3 base/instruction variants.
evaluations.metric: Linear, TV and JS dissimilarity peaks.
evaluations.result: Instruction-tuned models reveal the intended threshold; Pythia reveals a tokenizer boundary instead.
evaluations.baseline: Base versus instruction models and alternative divergence/window choices.

evaluations.setting: Pythia-70M temperature sweep for ten-token completions.
evaluations.result: Two prompt-specific peaks delimit three qualitative regimes, including negative heat-capacity behavior.
evaluations.baseline: A unigram frequency model shows that the upper-temperature crossover is not uniquely transformer-driven.

evaluations.setting: Pythia checkpoints and QKV weight histograms.
evaluations.metric: Dissimilarity versus training epoch over random and short prompts.
evaluations.result: Some output and weight changes coincide, but locations depend on prompt and window length and several peaks are transient outliers.
evaluations.baseline: Weight-only distributions, OpenWebText prompts and seven short prompts.

limitations: A peak detects change but does not identify whether its cause is knowledge, tokenization, sampling or a training instability.
Experiments use models up to roughly 8B and short generated sequences.
Temperature findings are strongly prompt-dependent and sometimes crossovers rather than thermodynamic phase transitions.
Probability access makes the method gray-box; classifier density-ratio estimation is needed for API-only models.
Sampling requirements are large at each grid point and scale poorly across prompts and parameters.
Local maxima and window length require analyst choices and can confuse one-point outliers with persistent phases.
failure_modes: A tokenizer boundary produces a strong peak misread as semantic emergence.
A discontinuous metric, grid or checkpoint artifact creates apparent abruptness.
A capability changes without appreciably changing the sampled output distribution.
A rare safety-relevant behavior is diluted by generic prompt averaging.
Uncalibrated sequence probabilities distort density-ratio estimates.
reusable_insights: Treat transition detection as triage: every peak needs causal and semantic diagnosis.
Vary window length to distinguish persistent distribution shifts from isolated outliers.
Audit tokenization and sampling policy before attributing a peak to learned cognition.
Continuous distributional metrics complement, but do not replace, task-specific success metrics and internal analysis.
open_questions: Can transition scans predict capability acquisition before benchmark accuracy changes?
How can the method cover API-only models and rare behaviors efficiently?
Which peaks replicate across prompts, seeds, tokenizers and model families?
Can causal interventions map generic output transitions to internal circuits?

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. tie a sudden in-context-learning change to induction-head formation using internal analysis; the reviewed method is more task-agnostic and output-only but cannot itself identify a mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
competitive_landscape.difference: This work shows discontinuous task metrics can fabricate emergence; the reviewed paper explicitly uses continuous distributional distances, yet still must distinguish tokenizer, grid and crossover artifacts.

competitive_landscape.title: Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models Across Training and Scaling
competitive_landscape.difference: Pythia supplies controlled models and 154 checkpoints; the reviewed paper contributes a generic output-distribution change detector applied to that resource.

competitive_landscape.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: The emergence paper catalogs task-level scaling discontinuities across model size; the reviewed method scans any one-dimensional control parameter and does not require a preselected correctness metric.

novelty_assessment: Adapting f-divergence change-point estimators to tractable LLM sequence distributions is versatile and genuinely less task-engineered than benchmark metrics. The experiments also responsibly show why detection is not interpretation: tokenizer boundaries, finite-temperature crossovers and isolated checkpoints all produce peaks.
reviewer_notes: Read all 21 pages, including estimators, prompt/temperature/checkpoint experiments, sampling counts, implementation and Fisher-information appendices. Four primary emergence/training-dynamics comparators were checked on 2026-08-23.
